summary:
Lagos State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 does not stop at marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Sexual orientation carries exposure before arrival. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Those religious provisions do not operate in Lagos, but they govern onward travel within Nigeria.

Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, while gender expression remains exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers they face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions under the 2014 Act, and death-penalty risk under Sharia criminal law in some states. The advisory applies to entry into Lagos in full.

Lethal violence against trans people is recorded at national level, with no state-specific divergence recorded for Lagos. In August 2024 the beaten body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' was found along a highway in Abuja, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; she had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker and had expressed fear for her life in the previous year. Police stated that preliminary investigations revealed the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Lagos police conduct supplies the clearest enforcement example. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Detention adds a further exposure. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
No regional protective statute, recorded incident series or documented enforcement divergence from the national framework has been recorded for Lagos. The 2014 Act sits on top of colonial-era criminalisation rather than replacing it, and the country maintains no anti-discrimination protection for LGBTQ+ people at any level of government.

The religious criminal layer is uneven across the country. Sharia law applies to same-sex acts in all twelve states that operate it, carrying death-penalty exposure for male sodomy, while Lagos falls under secular criminal law alone with a 14-year ceiling. Travel between the two legal environments changes the risk category rather than the underlying criminalisation.

Unenacted legislative proposals remain a live source of uncertainty for gender expression. Reuters reported in September 2022 that proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing were circulating and that transgender Nigerians feared them; the sources available do not settle whether any such proposal has become law.

The corrections system's own review process produced a finding against the state. The October 2024 investigative panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had surrounded Bobrisky's detention while simultaneously finding that her placement in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, since she was a first-time offender.

Extortion and opportunistic violence function alongside the statute. The Lagos police assault and bribe demand recorded in March 2025, and the app-based kito gang operations recorded in April 2024, both proceeded without reference to any charge being laid, which indicates risk that does not require an SSMPA prosecution to materialise.
localsOnly:
Lagos residents live under the same national statute as visitors, with no state-level protection, exemption or recorded enforcement divergence. The Nigeria Police Force in Lagos has used the appearance of gayness as grounds for stop, assault and extorted release, as in the March 2025 case of Okafor, who was struck with a gun butt and freed after paying part of a 50,000 naira demand.

Community members face abduction and blackmail through dating platforms. Kito gangs use Grindr and similar apps to arrange meetings, then beat, film and threaten victims with outing, a pattern documented across Nigeria in April 2024 and applicable to residents of Lagos who rely on those platforms for social contact.

Trans residents are processed through the corrections system on ordinary offences and their housing placement is discretionary. Bobrisky's six-month term for naira abuse, served in a maximum-security Lagos prison from 12 April to 5 August 2024, prompted press speculation about which prison would hold her and a panel finding that the placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

The killing of 'Abuja Area Mama' in August 2024 shows how official identification of a trans victim is framed: police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and no suspects had been charged six months later. Residents of Lagos face the same investigative posture in cases of violence against them.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved. The sources available record the proposals and the fear they generated in September 2022 but do not establish their current legislative status, which matters for gender expression in Lagos.

No Lagos-specific prosecution figures, arrest tallies or court outcomes under the 2014 Act are sourced here. The evidence for enforcement in Lagos rests on individual reported incidents, principally the March 2025 police assault and the corrections handling of Bobrisky, rather than on any documented case series.

Whether a trans visitor detained in Lagos would be housed in a gender-congruent unit is not resolved beyond the Bobrisky matter. The October 2024 panel addressed security classification, not section placement, and no source describes the operational rule governing male or female wings.

Entry and border screening questions are not sourced: nothing in the inventory addresses how immigration officers treat mismatched identity documents, prior gender markers, or possession of hormone medication at Lagos airports.

Availability of trans-specific healthcare, shelters, safe accommodation and legal aid in Lagos is not addressed by any source in this inventory, and no complaints mechanism or redress route for victims of police extortion is documented.
